prompt: Which statement agrees with the Hückel criteria for aromaticity?

choices.text: An ion can be aromatic, and its π electrons need not equal its number of ring atoms
An aromatic species must be neutral, with no charge on any ring atom
choices.why: Nothing in the definition requires neutrality; the cyclopentadienyl anion and the cycloheptatrienyl cation are aromatic.

choices.text: An aromatic ring must be six-membered, like benzene's
choices.why: The cyclopentadienyl anion (five carbons) and the cycloheptatrienyl cation (seven carbons) are aromatic without a six-membered ring.

choices.text: The number of π electrons must equal the number of ring atoms
choices.why: The cyclopentadienyl anion has six π electrons in five p orbitals and is aromatic.

explanation: A molecule must be cyclic, conjugated (nearly planar with a p orbital on each atom) and have 4n + 2 π electrons. Nothing in this definition says that the number of π electrons must equal the number of ring atoms or that the substance must be neutral.

prompt: How many π electrons does the cyclopentadienyl anion, C5H5−, have?
explanation: Removing H+ from the CH2 group of 1,3-cyclopentadiene leaves both C–H electrons behind. The four electrons of the two double bonds plus that lone pair give six π electrons in five p orbitals, a Hückel number (n = 1).

prompt: How is the cyclopentadienyl anion formed from 1,3-cyclopentadiene?

choices.text: By removing H+ (with no electrons) from the CH2 carbon
By removing a hydride ion, H:^−, from the CH2 carbon
choices.why: Removing the hydrogen with both electrons leaves a carbocation, the four-π-electron cyclopentadienyl cation.

choices.text: By removing a hydrogen atom, H·, from the CH2 carbon
choices.why: Removing the hydrogen with one electron leaves the five-π-electron cyclopentadienyl radical.

choices.text: By adding H+ to one of the double bonds
choices.why: Adding a proton would give a positive ion, not an anion. The anion forms when H+ is removed.

explanation: Removing the hydrogen with no electrons (as H+) leaves a carbanion. When that carbon rehybridizes from sp3 to sp2, the ring is fully conjugated with six π electrons. Figure 15.4.2 shows the anion made by treating 1,3-cyclopentadiene with sodium hydroxide.

prompt: How is the cycloheptatrienyl cation formed from 1,3,5-cycloheptatriene?

choices.text: By removing a hydride ion, H:^−, from the CH2 carbon
By removing H+ from the CH2 carbon
choices.why: Removing H+ leaves the electron pair behind, giving the eight-π-electron cycloheptatrienyl anion.

choices.text: By removing a hydrogen atom, H·, from the CH2 carbon
choices.why: Removing H· gives the seven-π-electron cycloheptatrienyl radical.

choices.text: By adding an electron to the ring
choices.why: Adding electrons makes a negative ion. The cation forms when the hydrogen leaves with both electrons.

explanation: Removing the hydrogen with both electrons (H:^−) leaves a carbocation whose six π electrons, from the three double bonds, spread over seven p orbitals. The cation was first made more than a century ago by reaction of 1,3,5-cycloheptatriene with Br2.

prompt: After a hydrogen is removed from the CH2 carbon of 1,3-cyclopentadiene, what must that carbon do for the ring to become fully conjugated?

choices.text: Rehybridize from sp3 to sp2, so every ring carbon has a p orbital
Rehybridize from sp2 to sp3
choices.why: The CH2 carbon starts out sp3; it must become sp2 to have a p orbital.

choices.text: Rehybridize from sp2 to sp
choices.why: The CH2 carbon starts out sp3, and full conjugation needs it to become sp2.

choices.text: Stay sp3, since only the double-bond carbons need p orbitals
choices.why: Full conjugation needs a p orbital on every ring carbon.

explanation: In 1,3-cyclopentadiene and 1,3,5-cycloheptatriene, the CH2 carbon is saturated (sp3). Once a hydrogen is removed, if that carbon rehybridizes from sp3 to sp2, the product is fully conjugated, with a p orbital on every carbon.

prompt: How many π electrons does the cyclopentadienyl cation have?
explanation: Removing a hydride ion (H:^−) takes both C–H electrons, leaving only the four π electrons of the two double bonds. Four is a 4n number, so the 4n + 2 rule predicts the cation to be unstable; in practice it is highly reactive and difficult to prepare.

prompt: Which cyclopentadienyl species is easily prepared and remarkably stable?

choices.text: The anion, with six π electrons
The cation, with four π electrons
choices.why: The four-π-electron cation is highly reactive and difficult to prepare.

choices.text: The radical, with five π electrons
choices.why: The five-π-electron radical is highly reactive and shows no sign of aromatic stability.

choices.text: All three are about equally stable
choices.why: Only the anion has a Hückel number of π electrons; the cation and radical are highly reactive.

explanation: Both the four-π-electron cyclopentadienyl cation and the five-π-electron radical are highly reactive and difficult to prepare. The six-π-electron cyclopentadienyl anion, by contrast, is easily prepared and remarkably stable.

prompt: 1,3-Cyclopentadiene is one of the most acidic hydrocarbons known. What is its pKa?
explanation: The cyclopentadienyl anion is so stable and easily formed that 1,3-cyclopentadiene has pKa = 16, a value comparable to that of water.

prompt: Why is 1,3-cyclopentadiene (pKa = 16) so unusually acidic for a hydrocarbon?

choices.text: Losing H+ gives the aromatic six-π-electron cyclopentadienyl anion
Losing H+ gives an aromatic cation
choices.why: Losing H+ leaves a negative ion; the aromatic species formed is the anion.

choices.text: Its CH2 hydrogens are bonded to an sp carbon
choices.why: The CH2 carbon is sp3. The acidity comes from the stability of the anion that forms.

choices.text: Losing H+ gives a ring with four π electrons
choices.why: Losing H+ leaves the C–H electron pair in the ring, so the anion has six π electrons. The four-π-electron ring is the cation, formed by loss of a hydride ion.

explanation: The conjugate base, the cyclopentadienyl anion, has six π electrons in a cyclic conjugated ring and is aromatic. It is so stable and easily formed that the pKa of 1,3-cyclopentadiene is 16, comparable to water.

prompt: Which cycloheptatrienyl species is extraordinarily stable?

choices.text: The cation, with six π electrons
The radical, with seven π electrons
choices.why: The seven-π-electron radical is reactive and difficult to prepare.

choices.text: The anion, with eight π electrons
choices.why: Eight is a 4n number; the anion is reactive and difficult to prepare.

choices.text: The anion, with six π electrons
choices.why: Removing H+ leaves the electron pair in the ring, giving eight π electrons, not six. The six-π-electron species is the cation.

explanation: The seven-π-electron cycloheptatrienyl radical and the eight-π-electron anion are reactive and difficult to prepare, while the six-π-electron cycloheptatrienyl cation is extraordinarily stable. Six is a Hückel number (n = 1).

prompt: How many resonance structures can be drawn for the cyclopentadienyl anion?
explanation: The negative charge can be placed on each of the five ring carbons in turn, giving five equivalent resonance structures (Exercise 15.4.1). As a result, all the carbon–carbon bonds are equivalent.

prompt: How many absorption lines would you expect in the ^13C NMR spectrum of the cyclopentadienyl anion?
explanation: The anion's five resonance structures are equivalent, so all five carbons (and all five hydrogens) are equivalent. The anion shows one resonance line in both its ^1H and ^13C NMR spectra (Exercise 15.4.1).

prompt: What do electrostatic potential maps show about the cyclopentadienyl anion and the cycloheptatrienyl cation?

choices.text: Both ions are symmetrical, with the charge shared equally among all the ring atoms
The charge stays on the carbon that lost the hydrogen
choices.why: Cyclic conjugation spreads the charge evenly around the ring.

choices.text: The anion's charge is spread out, but the cation's stays on one carbon
choices.why: Both ions are symmetrical, with the charge equally shared among all atoms in each ring.

choices.text: The charge sits on the ring hydrogens
choices.why: The charge belongs to the π system of the ring and is shared equally among the ring atoms.

explanation: Figure 15.4.2 shows that both ions are symmetrical, with the charge equally shared among all the atoms in each ring, as expected for six π electrons in a cyclic conjugated system.

prompt: Cyclooctatetraene reacts readily with potassium metal to form the stable dianion C8H8^2−. What geometry do you expect for the dianion?

choices.text: Flat, because with 10 π electrons it is aromatic
Tub-shaped, like neutral cyclooctatetraene
choices.why: The dianion has 10 π electrons, a Hückel number, so it is aromatic and flat.

choices.text: Flat, because with 8 π electrons it is antiaromatic
choices.why: Two added electrons plus the original eight make 10 π electrons (n = 2), so the dianion is aromatic.

choices.text: Tub-shaped, because charged rings can't be aromatic
choices.why: Ions can be aromatic, as the cyclopentadienyl anion and cycloheptatrienyl cation show.

explanation: Potassium gives cyclooctatetraene two electrons, so the dianion has 8 + 2 = 10 π electrons, a Hückel number (4n + 2 with n = 2). The dianion is aromatic and flat, which is why it forms so easily (Exercise 15.4.2).

prompt: The cyclopentadienyl system has five π molecular orbitals: a single lowest-energy orbital with degenerate pairs above it. How many unpaired electrons does the four-π-electron cyclopentadienyl cation have?
explanation: Two electrons fill the single lowest orbital. The other two go into the next level, a degenerate pair, one in each orbital, so the cation has two unpaired electrons. The radical has one unpaired electron and the anion none (Exercise 15.4.3).
